title: Locks, atomics and concurrent collections
idea: Java gives you three tools for shared state: explicit locks for multi-field invariants, atomics for single lock-free variables, and concurrent collections for safe per-key updates.

analogy.text: A shared tally board. A lock is the one marker people pass around. An atomic is a clicker counter. A concurrent map is a board split into sections.
analogy.breaks: A clicker never fails; a compare-and-set can fail and must retry.

points: `ReentrantLock` does what `synchronized` does, plus `tryLock`, timeouts and fair ordering.
Locking several objects in one global order, such as by id, prevents deadlock.
Atomics update one variable without locks using compare-and-set, retrying when another thread wins.
`ConcurrentHashMap` makes `merge` and `compute` atomic per key; `get` then `put` stays racy.

steps.caption: Shared stock holds 2. Threads A and B each want one unit. No lock is taken.
B also reads 2 before A writes. With a plain `int`, both would now write 1.
A calls `compareAndSet(2, 1)`. Memory still holds 2, so the swap succeeds in one atomic step.
B calls `compareAndSet(2, 1)`. Memory now holds 1, not 2, so it returns false and writes nothing.
B loops and reads the fresh value: 1.
B calls `compareAndSet(1, 0)`. Nobody interfered this time, so it succeeds.
Two units sold, none lost, stock never negative. A third caller would see 0 and return false.

code.title: ReentrantLock transfer
code.caption: Two threads transfer in opposite directions 1,000 times each. Ordered locking keeps the total intact and avoids deadlock.

walk.text: Each account owns a private lock; the comment records which field it guards.
Even reads take the lock, so a reader never sees a half-finished transfer.
Lock the lower id first. Opposite transfers then queue instead of each holding one lock.
Both locks are held before any check, so check and update form one atomic step.
A failed check throws while locked; the `finally` blocks still release both locks.
Unlock in reverse order, always in `finally`; a missed unlock blocks every later caller.

code.title: Atomics and ConcurrentHashMap
code.caption: Eight threads try 160 reservations against 100 units. The compare-and-set loop never oversells; `merge` counts requests per SKU.

walk.text: Eight buyers, twenty attempts each, spread over three SKUs: more demand than stock.
`join` waits for every thread, so the printed totals are final and repeatable.
Each shared field is a thread-safe type and `final`; there is no lock anywhere.
`merge` reads, adds and writes one key atomically. `get` then `put` could lose counts.
The CAS loop: read, check for zero, swap only if nobody changed the value meanwhile.
`left` and `rejected` are separate atomics, so read them only after the threads finish.

pitfalls: Calling `lock()` without `unlock()` in `finally`: one exception leaves the lock held forever.
Two atomics updated separately are not atomic together; guard multi-field invariants with one lock.
Locking accounts in argument order deadlocks when two transfers run in opposite directions.

quiz.why: The first call finds 1 and swaps it to 0. The second expects 1, finds 0, returns false and writes nothing.

takeaway: One variable: an atomic. One map key: a concurrent map. Several fields: a lock.

starters: When should I pick ReentrantLock over synchronized?
Why does ConcurrentHashMap get then put still race?
When is an AtomicInteger slower than a lock?
